pl-l3d27c5-d1e115.summary: Turns to the mode of each love.

pl-l3d27c5-d1e118.summary: Quotes Augustine's divinely established rule: love God for his own sake with the whole heart, and neighbor as yourself, that is, toward and for the end you ought to love yourself; for you ought to love yourself in the good and for God (sentence continues).
claims: Neighbor is to be loved for the same end as oneself.

pl-l3d27c5-d1e127.summary: Completes the rule: so the neighbor too is to be loved in the good, not in evil, and for God.
claims: Neighbor is to be loved in the good and for God.

pl-l3d27c5-d1e131.summary: Holds that every man must be understood as neighbor, since no one is to be wronged. One should love men because they are just or that they may be just, in God or for God, and so love oneself too. Whoever loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, that is, for being evil, and so does not really love himself: whoever loves iniquity hates his soul.
claims: Men are to be loved as just or so that they may become just.
Loving oneself unjustly is in truth hating oneself.

pl-l3d27c5-d1e143.summary: Explains with Augustine that the mind is so made that it always remembers, understands, and loves itself; yet since one who hates another tries to harm him, the mind that harms itself is said to hate itself, willing what harms it without knowing. So whoever knows how to love himself loves God, while one who does not love God, though he loves himself by nature, can be said to hate himself, acting as his own enemy.
claims: The mind naturally always loves itself.
Whoever harms himself by sin hates himself.
To love oneself rightly is to love God.

pl-l3d27c5-d1e152.summary: Concludes that the mode of loving oneself must be commanded, so that self-love benefits oneself, though no sane man doubts that he loves himself and wishes his own good. The mode is given in 'as yourself': love the neighbor toward the end you love yourself. Since you ought to love yourself not for yourself but for God, the most right end of love, no one should resent being loved for God. Christ's 'love one another as I have loved you' shows the mode: for this end, that you be sons and have life.
claims: The mode of self-love must be commanded.
One ought to love oneself for God, not for oneself.
Christ's new commandment gives the end of love: sonship and life.

pl-l3d27c5-d1e167.summary: Explains the mode of loving God: with the whole heart (intellect), the whole soul (will), the whole mind (memory), so that all thoughts, life, and understanding are directed to him from whom we have them. No part of life is left free, but whatever comes to mind is swept toward where love runs. Loving God for his own sake is also a mode, so that, as some hold, there are two modes of loving God.
claims: To love God wholly is to direct intellect, will, and memory to him.
No part of life is exempt from the love of God.
Loving God for his own sake is a mode of loving him.

pl-l3d27c5.summary: Sets out the mode of both loves following Augustine. Love God for his own sake with the whole heart, and neighbor as yourself, that is, for the end for which you ought to love yourself: in the good and for God. Every man is neighbor. One who loves himself unjustly hates his soul; the mind naturally remembers, understands, and loves itself, yet one who does not love God harms and so hates himself. The mode of self-love must be commanded, and Christ's 'as I have loved you' gives its end, that we be sons and have life. The mode of loving God, 'with whole heart, soul, and mind', means intellect, will, and memory, so that no part of life is left idle; loving God for his own sake is also a mode.
claims: Neighbor is to be loved as oneself: in the good and for God.
One who loves iniquity hates his own soul.
The mode of self-love must be commanded.
To love God with heart, soul, and mind is to love him with intellect, will, and memory.
